blurb: From Turing and Dartmouth through two AI winters to deep learning and the LLM era.

steps.p: In 1950, Alan Turing's paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" asked whether machines can think and proposed the imitation game.
The 1956 Dartmouth workshop gathered the founders of the field, under the name "artificial intelligence".
Programs proved theorems, played checkers and held simple conversations. Many predicted human-level AI within a generation.

cards.aside: The optimism of the 1950s and 60s set up the disappointments that followed.

cards.why: John McCarthy, in the 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth workshop, written with Minsky, Rochester and Shannon. McCarthy later created the Lisp programming language.

cards.statement: The Dartmouth proposal suggested significant progress could be made in a single summer.
cards.why: True. It proposed that a carefully selected group of scientists could make a significant advance on making machines use language and form abstractions over one summer.

options: A machine can beat a human at chess
A judge, chatting by text, can tell a machine from a human
A machine can copy a painting
A computer can imitate another computer
cards.why: Indistinguishability in conversation. Turing replaced "can machines think?" with a practical test. It is now known as the Turing test.

cards.title: ELIZA's creator was disturbed when his own secretary asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it privately.
cards.detail: Joseph Weizenbaum's 1966 program imitated a therapist by reflecting users' words back. People's emotional attachment to such a simple trick turned him into a lifelong critic of AI hype.

cards.statement: ELIZA understood the meaning of what users typed.
cards.why: False. It matched keywords and rearranged sentences using scripts, such as turning "I am sad" into "Why are you sad?". There was no understanding at all.

cards.title: Boom and bust

steps.p: By the mid-1970s, promises had outrun results. Critical reviews led governments to slash funding.
In the 1980s, companies built systems encoding experts' knowledge as thousands of if-then rules.
Rule systems proved brittle and expensive to maintain. The market for specialized AI hardware collapsed in the late 1980s.

cards.aside: Each winter followed a gap between what was promised and what was delivered.

cards.q: The 1973 Lighthill Report in the UK led to…
options: Deep cuts to AI research funding
cards.why: Funding cuts. Mathematician James Lighthill concluded AI had failed to meet its grand objectives, and British support for AI research collapsed for years.

cards.q: Expert systems of the 1980s worked by…
options: Applying large sets of hand-written if-then rules from human experts
cards.why: Hand-coded rules. Knowledge engineers interviewed experts and wrote rules. Every new situation needed new rules, which made the systems brittle.

cards.title: DEC's XCON expert system configured computer orders and was reported to save the company around $25 million a year.
cards.detail: It checked that each VAX computer order had compatible components. Its success fueled the 1980s expert system boom, but it needed constant maintenance as products changed.

cards.statement: IBM's Deep Blue, which beat Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, was a neural network.
cards.why: False. Deep Blue used custom chips to search about 200 million positions per second with a hand-tuned evaluation function. It learned nothing on its own.

cards.statement: Neural network research continued through the AI winters, even when it was unfashionable.
cards.why: True. Researchers like Hinton, LeCun and Bengio kept working on it through the 1990s and 2000s, when much of the field favored other methods.

cards.title: Three ingredients arrive together

steps.p: The internet produced enormous datasets, and ImageNet (2009) gave vision researchers millions of labeled images.
GPUs made training large networks practical.
ReLU activations, dropout and better initialization made deep networks trainable. AlexNet's 2012 win combined everything.

cards.aside: Most ideas were decades old; what changed was the scale available to test them.

cards.q: The 2018 Turing Award, computing's top honor, went to which three deep learning pioneers?
cards.why: Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio, often called the godfathers of deep learning, for work that made deep neural networks practical.

cards.statement: Yann LeCun's convolutional networks were reading handwritten checks commercially in the 1990s.
cards.why: True. LeNet-based systems from AT&T Bell Labs processed a significant share of US checks by the late 1990s — long before deep learning was fashionable.

cards.q: Who led the creation of the ImageNet dataset?
cards.why: Fei-Fei Li, then at Princeton and later Stanford. Her team used crowd workers to label millions of images, betting that data was the missing ingredient.

cards.title: Geoffrey Hinton and John Hopfield won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for foundational work on neural networks.
cards.detail: The prize recognized Hopfield networks and Hinton's Boltzmann machines, which drew on ideas from statistical physics.

cards.q: The "deep" in deep learning refers to…
cards.why: Many layers. Depth lets networks build complex features from simpler ones, layer upon layer.

cards.title: 2017 to now

steps.p: The transformer (2017) was followed by GPT and BERT (2018), showing pretraining on raw text transfers to many tasks.
GPT-3 (2020) showed sheer scale brought few-shot learning. ChatGPT (2022) put it in front of the public.
GPT-4 (2023), multimodal models, reasoning models (2024) and agents followed in quick succession.

cards.aside: In under a decade, language models went from research curiosity to a technology used by hundreds of millions.

cards.q: Which is the correct chronological order?
cards.why: BERT (2018) → GPT-3 (2020) → ChatGPT (2022) → o1 (2024). Each step took about two years.

cards.statement: In 2019, OpenAI initially withheld the full GPT-2 model over concerns about misuse.
cards.why: True. It released GPT-2 in stages over nine months. Critics called it hype; others saw it as an early experiment in responsible release.

cards.title: GPT-3 had about 1,500 times more parameters than GPT-1, just two years earlier.
cards.detail: GPT-1 (2018) had 117 million parameters; GPT-3 (2020) had 175 billion. That pace of scaling was unprecedented in computing.

cards.q: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for…
cards.why: AlphaFold. They shared the prize with David Baker, honored for computational protein design.

cards.title: Read the paper that started it
cards.body: Turing's 1950 paper is short, witty and readable. He anticipated objections still argued today, including that machines can only do what they are told.
cards.challenge: Read the "Learning Machines" section of Turing's "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" — about ten minutes.
